## Development

### Running Tests

```bash
mise run test
```

### Running Integration Tests

```bash
mise run test:integration
```

### Running the Windows Installer Tests

`scripts/install.ps1` has its own Pester suite and PSScriptAnalyzer pass under
`scripts/test/`; `.github/workflows/install-ps1-e2e.yml` runs it in both
Windows PowerShell 5.1 and pwsh on PRs that touch the installer or its tests,
followed by a real install on a Windows runner, and `mise run test:ps1` runs
the suite locally when `pwsh` is installed (it skips cleanly otherwise; it is
not part of `check`). On a fresh machine run
`scripts/test/init.ps1` once first: it installs Pester and PSScriptAnalyzer for
the current user and, on Windows PowerShell 5.1, the NuGet package provider
that `Install-Module` needs there.

### Running All Tests (CI)

```bash
mise run test:ci
```

This runs unit tests, integration tests, and the E2E canary (Vogon agent) in sequence. Integration tests use the `//go:build integration` build tag and are located in `cmd/entire/cli/integration_test/`.

### Running E2E Canary Tests (Vogon Agent)

The Vogon agent is a deterministic fake agent that exercises the full E2E test suite without making any API calls.

```bash
mise run test:e2e:canary           # Run all E2E tests with the Vogon agent
mise run test:e2e:canary TestFoo   # Run a specific test
```

- **Runs as part of `test:ci`** — canary failures block merges
- **No API calls, no cost** — safe to run freely, unlike real agent E2E tests
- **If a canary test fails, the bug is in the CLI or test infrastructure**, not in an agent
- Located in `e2e/vogon/` (binary) and `cmd/entire/cli/agent/vogon/` (Agent interface)
- The binary parses prompts via regex, creates/modifies/deletes files, and fires lifecycle hooks
- **IMPORTANT: When changing E2E test prompt wording**, the Vogon binary (`e2e/vogon/main.go`) parses prompts with hardcoded regexes. New phrasing may not match existing patterns — always run `mise run test:e2e:canary` after changing prompt text and fix Vogon's parsing if tests fail.

### Running E2E Tests (Only When Explicitly Requested)

**IMPORTANT: Do NOT run E2E tests proactively.** E2E tests make real API calls to agents, which consume tokens and cost money. Only run them when the user explicitly asks for E2E testing.

```bash
mise run test:e2e [filter]                          # All agents, filtered
mise run test:e2e --agent claude-code [filter]       # Claude Code only as an example here, replace `claude-code` with other agents to run tests for those agents
```

E2E tests:

- Use the `//go:build e2e` build tag
- Located in `e2e/tests/`
- See [`e2e/README.md`](e2e/README.md) for full documentation (structure, debugging, adding agents)
- Test real agent interactions (Claude Code, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Cursor, Factory AI Droid, Copilot CLI, Pi, or Vogon creating files, committing, etc.)
- Validate checkpoint scenarios documented in `docs/architecture/checkpoint-scenarios.md`
- Support multiple agents via `E2E_AGENT` env var (`claude-code`, `gemini`, `opencode`, `cursor`, `factoryai-droid`, `copilot-cli`, `pi`, `vogon`)

**Environment variables:**

- `E2E_AGENT` - Agent to test with (default: `claude-code`)
- `E2E_CLAUDE_MODEL` - Claude model to use (default: `haiku` for cost efficiency)
- `E2E_TIMEOUT` - Per-prompt timeout, overriding each runner's own default (e.g. `E2E_TIMEOUT=4m`)

The per-prompt default is the runner's, not a single number: codex, copilot-cli and gemini use 60s, cursor 90s, opencode 2m, and claude-code, droid, pi, vogon and roger-roger impose no per-prompt bound at all — for those the scenario timeout passed to `ForEachAgent` is the only deadline. `E2E_TIMEOUT` sets a bound for every runner including those, and a per-test `agents.WithPromptTimeout(...)` overrides it. All ten resolve through `promptTimeout` in `e2e/agents/agent.go`; a runner that resolves its own is a build failure (`TestEveryRunPromptResolvesThroughPromptTimeout`). A malformed value is an error rather than a silent fall back to the default.

### Test Parallelization

**Always use `t.Parallel()` in tests.** Every top-level test function and subtest should call `t.Parallel()` unless it modifies process-global state (e.g., `os.Chdir()`).

```go
func TestFeature_Foo(t *testing.T) {
    t.Parallel()
    // ...
}

// Integration tests with TestEnv
func TestFeature_Bar(t *testing.T) {
    t.Parallel()
    env := NewFeatureBranchEnv(t)
    // ...
}
```

**Exception:** Tests that modify process-global state cannot be parallelized. This includes `os.Chdir()`/`t.Chdir()` and `os.Setenv()`/`t.Setenv()` — Go's test framework will panic if these are used after `t.Parallel()`.

### Git in Tests

**Tests that touch git state must use an isolated temp repo — never the real repo CWD.**

Many handlers (lifecycle, strategy, hooks) resolve the git repo from CWD via `OpenRepository`, `GetGitCommonDir`, `DetectFileChanges`, etc. Without isolation, tests can create session state files, shadow branches, or other artifacts in the real `.git/` directory.

Use the `testutil` helpers:

```go
tmpDir := t.TempDir()
testutil.InitRepo(t, tmpDir)                    // git init + user config + disable GPG
testutil.WriteFile(t, tmpDir, "f.txt", "init")  // create a file
testutil.GitAdd(t, tmpDir, "f.txt")             // stage it
testutil.GitCommit(t, tmpDir, "init")           // commit (needs at least one commit for HEAD)
t.Chdir(tmpDir)                                 // redirect CWD-based git resolution
```

`testutil.InitRepo` configures `user.name`, `user.email`, and disables GPG signing — safe for CI environments without global git config.

**Prefer `testutil.InitRepo()` over direct `git.PlainInit()` in tests.** When a test in this repo needs an initialized repository, use `testutil.InitRepo(t, dir)` unless the test specifically needs lower-level initialization behavior that the helper cannot provide. Do not call `git.PlainInit()` directly and then create commits or run CLI git operations without also reproducing the helper's repo-local config.

**Do NOT** shell out to `git init`/`git commit` directly without setting user config and `--no-gpg-sign`, and **do NOT** run lifecycle/strategy handlers from the real repo CWD in tests.

### Config/Cache/Keyring Isolation in Tests

Tests must never read or write the developer's real `~/.config/entire`
(contexts.json, version_check.json), `~/.cache/entire` (nodes.json,
cluster_cores.json, api_discovery.json), or OS keychain. The developer may be
using `entire` for real while tests run.

- **Single resolver**: `internal/entireclient/userdirs` is the only place
  that resolves the per-user config dir (`userdirs.Config()`:
  `$ENTIRE_CONFIG_DIR` else `~/.config/entire`) and cache dir
  (`userdirs.Cache()`: `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/entire` else `~/.cache/entire`).
  Never derive these paths anywhere else.
- **In-process safety net**: `userdirs` and the `tokenstore` default backend
  detect `go test` (via `internal/testdirs`) and fall back to a throwaway
  per-process temp directory when their env override is unset. The fallback
  is shared across tests in one process — for per-test isolation still set
  `t.Setenv("ENTIRE_CONFIG_DIR", t.TempDir())` and
  `tokenstore.UseFileBackendForTesting(...)`.
- **Spawned binaries are NOT covered**: `testing.Testing()` is false in a
  subprocess. The integration and e2e TestMains set `ENTIRE_CONFIG_DIR`,
  `XDG_CACHE_HOME`, `ENTIRE_TOKEN_STORE=file`, `ENTIRE_TOKEN_STORE_PATH`, and
  `ENTIRE_TEST_AUTH_STORE_FILE` process-wide so every spawned `entire` (and
  every agent-invoked hook) inherits isolation. Any new harness that spawns
  the real binary must do the same.
- **Legacy auth store**: `auth.NewStore()` talks straight to the zalando
  keyring; packages whose tests can reach it need `keyring.MockInit()` in
  `TestMain` (see `cmd/entire/cli/global_test.go`) — the `testdirs` fallback
  does not cover it in-process.

### Spawning subprocesses in tests (TTY detection)

Tests that spawn the real `entire` or `git` binary need the child to be non-interactive so prompts don't hang on a developer terminal.

`interactive.CanPromptInteractively()` resolves in this order:

1. `ENTIRE_TEST_TTY=1` → force interactive ON (any other non-empty value → force OFF).
2. `testing.Testing()` → false. In-process `go test` runs are non-interactive by default; no per-test `t.Setenv("ENTIRE_TEST_TTY", "0")` is needed.
3. Agent sentinels → false. `interactive.agentSubprocessEnvVars` is the single
   source of truth for the presence-checked ones (`COPILOT_CLI`, `CURSOR_AGENT`,
   `GEMINI_CLI`, `OPENCODE`, `PI_CODING_AGENT`) — the function reads it and the
   tests both enumerate and clear it, so adding a vendor is a one-line change.
   `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0` stays separate because only that exact value counts.
   `CLAUDECODE` is deliberately not a sentinel: Claude Code sets it, but adding
   it withdraws prompts from the largest agent population at once, which is a
   product decision rather than a detection fix.
4. `CI=<non-empty-non-false>` → false.
5. Controlling-terminal probe — `/dev/tty` on Unix, `CONIN$` + `CONOUT$` on
   Windows. A terminal held in raw mode (canonical/line input off) belongs to a
   full-screen TUI that spawned us, not to a shell we can prompt: TUI git clients
   (lazygit, gitui, tig) run `git commit` as a child while owning the screen, so
   the hook inherits the same terminal it must not prompt on. The mode check
   fails open when it cannot read the mode. See `interactive/tty_*.go` and
   `interactive/rawmode_{unix,windows}.go` for the platform split and rationale.

For subprocesses spawning the real `entire` binary (e2e, integration tests, `entire` calling itself from a hook), prefer `execx.NonInteractive` over env-var plumbing:

```go
import "github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/execx"

cmd := execx.NonInteractive(ctx, getTestBinary(), "status")
cmd.Dir = repoDir
out, err := cmd.CombinedOutput()
```

`execx.NonInteractive` puts the child in a new session with no controlling terminal (`Setsid` on Unix, `DETACHED_PROCESS | CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP` on Windows), so the child's platform terminal probe fails naturally. No env var required.

`interactive.UnderTest()` returns true when `testing.Testing()` or `ENTIRE_TEST_TTY` is set — use it where code needs to skip a real-terminal operation even if `CanPromptInteractively()` returns true (e.g., opening `interactive.OpenPromptTTY()` directly inside a prompt reader).

### Linting and Formatting

```bash
mise run fmt && mise run lint
```

`mise run fmt` can rewrite files. Treat `mise run fmt && mise run lint` as a single verification sequence: if formatting changes anything, run lint again on the formatted tree rather than assuming a previous lint result still applies.

### Before Every Commit (REQUIRED)

**CI will fail if you skip these steps:**

```bash
mise run check
```

Equivalent expanded form:

```bash
mise run fmt      # Format code (CI enforces gofmt)
mise run lint     # Lint check (CI enforces golangci-lint)
mise run test:ci  # Run all tests (unit + integration)
```

`mise run check` runs the three commands above.

Safety note: do not treat a clean `mise run lint` result as final unless it was run after the most recent `mise run fmt` pass.

### Before Any Push Or Remote Code Update (REQUIRED)

Before pushing commits or otherwise sending code changes to any remote, run `mise run lint` on the current tree and ensure it passes. If `mise run fmt` changed files, rerun `mise run lint` on the formatted tree before pushing.

**Common CI failures from skipping this:**

- `gofmt` formatting differences → run `mise run fmt`
- Lint errors → run `mise run lint` and fix issues
- Test failures → run `mise run test` and fix

### Source-Level Guard Tests

Four tests scan this repo's own source with `git grep` to enforce an invariant
the compiler cannot: `TestRootBasesAreTrusted` (root bases are trusted paths),
`TestTranscriptReadsOnlyShrink` (the unconfined transcript-read ratchet),
`TestGitStatusCallSitesPassNoOptionalLocks`, and
`TestAllHookConfigRelPaths_CoversEveryWorktreeConfigAgent`.

**They all go through `testutil.GitGrepGuard`, which owns three flags.** Each was
missing from at least one guard, and the same one was missing from three:

- `--untracked`. `git grep` searches the INDEX. Every one of these guards has
  "someone just added a file" as its subject, so the file it most needs to see is
  the one not yet staged. Two failure shapes were worse than a miss: the
  hook-config guard compares two sets built from the same blind grep, so a new
  agent package calling `OpenHookConfig` without declaring `HookConfigRelPath`
  was absent from both and the comparison *passed*; and the root-base guard's
  staleness half reported a just-added entry as STALE, telling the author to
  delete the entry that legitimised their new root.
- `--no-color`. `color.ui`/`color.grep` set to `always` colorizes into a pipe and
  the escapes land in the **filename** field. True of `-l` too, which looks
  immune. Guards then either misparse (read as staleness, #2248) or compare
  garbage to garbage while their "did we match anything" assertion still passes.
- Repo-selector scrubbing. Git exports `GIT_DIR`/`GIT_WORK_TREE` to hooks and
  they outrank `cmd.Dir`, so a `go test` under a hook or `git rebase --exec`
  scanned a different repository. `RunGit`'s isolation does **not** cover this:
  it filters `GIT_CONFIG_*` only.

Two rules for writing one:

- **A pathspec restricted to `*.go`, so an unparseable path can be fatal.** The
  `git status` guard passed a bare `cmd internal`, which also matched testdata
  `.jsonl` and a `.md`, so its non-`.go` branch had to `continue` — and that
  skip was the only thing between colorized output and a guard that silently
  checked nothing.
- **Fail on zero matches.** A detection pattern that goes stale otherwise passes
  forever. `GitGrepGuard` does this itself; the `checked == 0` tallies are the
  second half of the same idea.

### Code Duplication Prevention

Before implementing Go code, use `/go:discover-related` to find existing utilities and patterns that might be reusable.

**Check for duplication:**

```bash
mise run dup           # Comprehensive check (threshold 50) with summary
mise run dup:staged    # Check only staged files
mise run lint          # Normal lint includes dupl at threshold 75 (new issues only)
mise run lint:full     # All issues at threshold 75
```

**Tiered thresholds:**

- **75 tokens** (lint/CI) - Blocks on serious duplication (~20+ lines)
- **50 tokens** (dup) - Advisory, catches smaller patterns (~10+ lines)

When duplication is found:

1. Check if a helper already exists in `common.go` or nearby utility files
2. If not, consider extracting the duplicated logic to a shared helper
3. If duplication is intentional (e.g., test setup), add a `//nolint:dupl` comment with explanation

The CLI uses a specific pattern for error output to avoid duplication between Cobra and main.go.

**How it works:**

- `root.go` sets `SilenceErrors: true` globally - Cobra never prints errors

description: Audit and safely prepare a Git repository for an Entire-centered task workflow. Use this before creating a Trail or task worktree, when entering an unfamiliar repository, when origin/upstream ownership may be confused, or when checking Entire, Graph, runner, checkpoint, mirror, authentication, and push-safety prerequisites. # Repository Bootstrap

Establish trustworthy repository facts before task automation depends on them. A
wrong repository identity can create a Trail in the canonical project, publish a
branch to the wrong owner, or associate checkpoint history with the wrong task.

This skill is a repository boundary. By default it does not create task
branches, worktrees, Trails, commits, pushes, pull requests, initial commits, or
runner files. Runner onboarding is the one separately approved exception: after
the audit, the skill may invoke the supported `entire runner setup` interface,
then verify the files without staging or committing them.

## Command

Use the bundled script from the repository or directory being inspected:

```bash
bash <skill-dir>/scripts/repository-bootstrap check --repo .
```

The same script supports both repository shapes:

- In a conventional checkout containing `.git`, pass the checkout root.
- In a bare-worktree setup, pass a linked worktree to obtain the complete audit.
- Passing the container whose `.git` points at `.bare` is also supported. The
  result includes shared Git facts and linked-worktree candidates, marks

# Commit

Stage relevant changes and create a commit using the conventional commits format.
Always use this skill instead of running `git commit` directly — this ensures
the message format is consistent across every tool (OpenCode, Claude Code, Codex).

## When to Use

- **Invoke** (`/commit`) after completing every task — this is the final step of every task
- **Invoke** (`/commit --push`) to commit and push in one step
- **AI must use this skill** whenever a commit is needed — never run `git commit -m` directly
- **AI should suggest** when: user says "commit", "save my changes", "checkpoint",
  "commit this", "commit and push", "push my changes", or a task's acceptance criteria say "committed using /commit skill"

## Commit Message Format

```
<type>(<scope>): <description>
```

**Types:**
- `feat` — new feature or capability
- `fix` — bug fix
- `chore` — build, config, dependency, tooling change (no production code change)
- `docs` — documentation only
- `test` — adding or updating tests
- `refactor` — code restructuring with no behaviour change
- `perf` — performance improvement

**Scope** is derived from the project structure. Use the most descriptive scope for the files changed. Scope is optional for small repos or when the change spans the whole repo.

**Examples:**
```
feat(api): add pagination to list endpoint
fix(auth): handle expired refresh tokens
test(search): add round-trip tests for index serialization
chore(ci): update release workflow
refactor(core): extract filter logic into separate function
docs: update CHANGELOG for new feature
```

## Steps

1. Run `git status` to see all changed/untracked files
2. Run `git diff --staged` (or `git diff` if nothing staged) to understand exactly what changed
3. Group related files — do not commit unrelated changes in one commit
4. Stage the relevant files: `git add <specific files>`
5. Draft a commit message following the format above
6. Show the message to the user and confirm before committing
7. Run `git commit -m "<message>"`

### Optional: Push (when `--push` is passed or user asks to push)

8. Push branch to remote:
   - If branch has no upstream: `git push -u origin <branch>`
   - Otherwise: `git push`
9. Run `git status` to verify clean state

## Rules

- **Always use this skill** — never run `git commit` directly without it
- `<type>(<scope>): <description>` — lowercase description, under 72 chars total
- No period at the end
- Description says what changed, not how (the diff shows how)
- **No task IDs, priority labels, or PRD metadata** — no "P0", "TASK-001:", "(PAG-004)"
- Do not stage secrets (`.env`, credentials files)
- Do not use force push
- Stage specific files — never blindly `git add .` without reviewing what's being staged
- **No Co-Authored-By trailers** — do not append `Co-Authored-By` lines to commit messages
- If unsure about the message, show 2-3 options and ask the user to pick

# Push Branch

Publish the current branch without changing history unexpectedly.

## Do

- Confirm the current branch is not the protected base branch.
- Check whether the branch already has an upstream.
- Resolve the exact outgoing commit range before pushing. For an existing
  upstream, compare its verified remote tip with `HEAD`. For a first publish,
  compare the verified branch base with `HEAD`. If the remote tip or branch base
  cannot be established reliably, report that uncertainty before pushing.
- Inspect every commit in that outgoing range for changes to `.entire`,
  `.codex`, `.claude`, `.opencode`, `AGENT.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `GEMINI.md`, or
  `CLAUDE.md`. Inspect commit history rather than only the final tree diff so a
  file that was added and later reverted is still disclosed.
- When outgoing commits touch any of those paths, show the exact paths and ask
  whether they are intentionally part of this push. Path names alone do not
  imply that a change is personal: runner configuration and agent instructions
  are often legitimate repository changes. Wait for a clear answer before
  pushing.
- If the user confirms the paths are intentional, continue with the normal push.
  Treat that answer as confirmation of those files only; it does not authorize a
  different remote, branch, force-push, or history rewrite.
- If the user says they are not intentional, stop before pushing and offer a
  separate remediation. Do not silently unstage files, drop commits, rewrite
  history, create branches, or add ignore rules.
- Keep worktree-only evidence separate. Untracked, staged, or unstaged changes
  that are not committed are not part of a push; leave them untouched and do not
  ask whether they are part of the outgoing push.
- Use a normal push for existing upstreams.
- Use `git push -u origin <branch>` for first publish.
- Do not force-push unless the user explicitly requested it.

## Output

- Branch pushed.
- Remote/upstream used.
- Any Entire or agent-configuration paths the user confirmed as intentional.
- Any push failure and the exact next action needed.

then verify the files without staging or committing them.

## Command

Use the bundled script from the repository or directory being inspected:

```bash

```

- In a conventional checkout containing `.git`, pass the checkout root.
- In a bare-worktree setup, pass a linked worktree to obtain the complete audit.

  result includes shared Git facts and linked-worktree candidates, marks
  worktree-local facts unresolved, and reports `select_repository_worktree`.

policy is `required`: an Entire-centered repository is expected to route normal
origin traffic through an `entire://` mirror while retaining direct GitHub access
as `github-origin`. A direct GitHub origin is reported as a decision, never
rewritten automatically.

Use `--mirror-policy optional` only when the user explicitly classifies a
repository as audit-only or defers mirror adoption. Add `--online` only when
live remote reachability is relevant; it performs non-interactive
`git ls-remote` probes and never fetches.

For machine-readable facts:

```bash

```

## Modes

### Check

Collect facts without changing files, Git configuration, refs, remotes,
authentication, or Entire state. Report:

- repository existence and conventional, bare, or bare-worktree layout;
- branch, HEAD, tracking branch, worktree count, commit presence, and dirty state;
- origin, github-origin, and upstream identities with credential-like URL userinfo redacted;
- whether upstream push is explicitly disabled;
- Entire enablement, local authentication status, Graph availability, committed
  runner count, worktree runner count, expected default-set validity, Git
  visibility, and ignore-rule provenance;
- configured checkpoint repository and any owner mismatch with origin;
- mirror topology and optional read reachability.

The check deliberately does not call `entire status`: that command can finalize
exited sessions and condense checkpoints. Entire enablement is read from the
worktree's settings files instead. Git dirty-state inspection disables optional
locks so it cannot refresh and rewrite the index.

For a bare container, `repository.worktree_state_resolved` is `false`,
`repository.requires_worktree` is `true`, and
`repository.worktree_candidates` lists the linked worktrees. In that result,
Entire enablement, checkpoint configuration, runner count, dirty state, and
current worktree branch are not evidence that those facts are absent; they are
`null` in JSON and unresolved until the check runs against a linked worktree.
The bare repository's symbolic `HEAD` is reported separately as
`git.default_branch`; it is never presented as a current worktree branch.

Interpret write access as `unproven`: a read-only probe cannot prove that a push
will be authorized.

## Missing runner decision

present on disk. When Entire is enabled and this count is zero, runner setup is
unfinished even if ignored or untracked JSON files happen to exist.

Use the other runner facts to distinguish the next action:

- `runner_state=missing` and `setup_repository_runners`: present the two
  supported setup choices below and ask which exact write the user approves.
- `runner_state=uncommitted-visible` and
  `review_and_commit_runner_configuration`: inspect the existing files instead
  of scaffolding around them. They are visible to Git but not committed.
- `runner_state=ignored-uncommitted` and `remediate_runner_ignore`: stop before
  setup or any success claim. Resolve the ignore decision first.
- `committed-files-missing` or `invalid`: report the corresponding repair
  decision. `runner_default_set_status=partial` only says the repository does
  not contain the whole embedded set; a deliberate custom subset can be valid,
  so inspect and report it without filling gaps by guessing runner types.

The CLI currently supports one embedded default set of six runner IDs:
`trail-confidence`, `trail-drift`, `trail-review`, `trail-risk`,
`trail-security`, and `trail-summary`. Use that set and the setup command; do
not invent runner types or hand-write replacement configs.

### Recommend a setup from repository evidence

Explain the recommendation from `runner_evidence`; it is advice, not approval.
The audit recommends repository-tailored setup when it finds signal the CLI can
use, such as `go.mod`, `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `README.md`, or meaningful
top-level structure. For a sparse/new repository, recommend generic defaults.
Let the user override either recommendation.

Present the implications before asking:

- **Generic six defaults** — `entire runner setup --defaults-only` creates the
  six functional embedded configs and stops. It makes no summary-provider call
  and does not gather tailoring-time remote history. The configs still name
  their normal runner runtime (currently `claude`); creation does not prove
  future runner-provider access.
- **Repository-tailored six** — `entire runner setup --yes` creates the same
  six, gathers repository signal, calls the selected summary provider once, and
  rewrites the prompt templates it can improve. Default gathering reads local
  repository/checkpoint evidence, uses `gh` for PR/issue history when available,
  and uses the authenticated Entire API for trail history when available. Those
  remote tiers are best-effort, but the gathered context and current templates
  are sent to the selected summary provider. If the user wants local repository
  signal only, offer `entire runner setup --yes --sources repo`; it still makes
  the one provider call. When no summary provider is configured, the CLI may
  select one and persist that selection locally; an explicit, verified
  `--agent <name>` chooses one for this run without saving it. Include that
  possible settings write in the approval discussion.

CLI verifies it is summary-capable. `--agent` chooses the text-generation agent
for this run; it is not a new runner type.

Show the exact repository path, exact command, expected six files, and the
provider/API implications. Ask for explicit approval and wait. A general request
to audit or bootstrap the repository is not approval to create runner files.

Immediately before an approved setup, re-run the check. It uses
`git check-ignore -v --no-index` against expected runner paths that are not
already tracked; tracked files remain visible regardless of an ignore rule,
while nonexistent pre-setup paths still expose rules that would hide newly
created files. If `runner_ignore_match` is non-empty:

1. Report the exact ignore source, line, pattern, and matched path.
2. Keep `remediate_runner_ignore` separate from runner setup and ask for
   separate approval for the proposed repository-owned fix.
3. For a global `.entire/` rule, prefer a narrow repository `.gitignore`
   exception that re-includes `.entire/`, `.entire/runners/`, and the JSON
   files when that matches repository policy. Do not edit global Git config.
4. Do not use `git add -f`, stage files, or claim ignored files are trackable.
5. Verify `git check-ignore -v --no-index` no longer matches, then present the
   runner setup approval again because the reviewed repository state changed.

run an unflagged interactive setup on the user's behalf:

```bash

# or
entire runner setup --yes
```

1. `runner_worktree_count` is six and every path in

   filename (`runner_default_set_status=complete`).
2. `runner_ignore_match` is empty and `runner_trackable=true`.

   status does not prove newly created files are visible.

   separately approved commit records them.

Do not call them committed, do not claim all six were tailored unless the setup
output and file changes prove that, and never report success for ignored files.

### Plan

Emit a deterministic, non-executable plan to stdout:

```bash
bash <skill-dir>/scripts/repository-bootstrap plan --repo . > /tmp/repo.plan
```

The plan contains a repository fingerprint and action identifiers, never shell
commands. It separates:

- `safe`: narrow protective Git configuration fixes supported by this draft;
- `decision`: work that needs repository intent or user confirmation;
- `unsafe`: contradictory identity or topology that blocks apply.

Generating a plan does not mutate the repository. Redirecting stdout to a plan
file is an explicit caller-side write outside the repository. When presenting a
plan to the user, reproduce the complete plan block—including
`ENTIRE_REPOSITORY_BOOTSTRAP_PLAN_V1` and its fingerprint—before interpreting
the actions. The version and fingerprint are part of the review contract, not
internal noise that can be summarized away.

### Apply

Apply only reviewed safe actions:

```bash
bash <skill-dir>/scripts/repository-bootstrap apply \
  --repo . \
  --plan /tmp/repo.plan \
  --yes \
  --allow disable_upstream_push
```

Apply requires all of the following:

1. an exact versioned plan header;
2. a fingerprint matching the repository's current facts;
3. `--yes`;
4. an individual `--allow <action-id>` for every safe action;
5. no unsafe item in the plan;
6. the action's live preconditions still hold.

The only safe actions in this draft are:

- `disable_upstream_push`: set `remote.upstream.pushurl` to `DISABLED` when upstream exists and is not already disabled;
- `set_origin_fetch_refspec`: add the ordinary heads refspec to a bare or bare-worktree repository when origin exists and has no fetch refspec.

Do not broaden apply by constructing commands from plan content or by using
`eval`. Unknown action identifiers are an error.

## Repository identity rules

- `origin` is the user's writable repository and owns Trails, task branches,
  checkpoints, runners, and builds.
- `upstream` is the canonical project. Its push URL must be `DISABLED`.
- Never query upstream as though it were the Trail repository.
- A configured checkpoint repository with a different owner from origin is not
  an automatic fix. Current Entire behavior may ignore it; report the mismatch
  and let the user choose a same-owner configuration or the origin default.
- The required Entire-centered topology is: `origin` is the `entire://` URL,
  `github-origin` is direct GitHub access to the same owner/repository, and
  `upstream` remains canonical and push-disabled.

  access. Prove that later with an explicitly authorized normal task-branch
  push, then verify the forwarded SHA through `github-origin`.
- Do not automatically route work to `entire/unmirrored/*` when GitHub is
  unavailable. That is a deliberate Entire-native publication choice.

## Decisions this skill never makes

Report these as decisions and stop before acting:

- initialize a repository or create its first commit;
- add, rename, remove, or rewrite a remote;
- enable Entire or install/adopt Graph;
- authenticate, change contexts, or prove write access;
- change checkpoint settings;
- adopt or remove a mirror, including renaming the existing origin;
- stage, stash, clean, reset, or otherwise alter dirty work;
- create a branch, worktree, Trail, checkpoint, build, PR, or comment;
- select a runner setup mode for the user, create runner files without the
  exact approval above, or stage/commit created runner files.

workflow. That workflow owns branch/worktree reuse, origin publication, Trail

- `1`: usage, dependency, stale-plan, or execution error.

Explain the recommendation from `runner_evidence`; it is advice, not approval.
The audit recommends repository-tailored setup when it finds signal the CLI can
use, such as `go.mod`, `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `README.md`, or meaningful
top-level structure. For a sparse/new repository, recommend generic defaults.
Let the user override either recommendation.

Present the implications before asking:

- **Generic six defaults** — `entire runner setup --defaults-only` creates the
  six functional embedded configs and stops. It makes no summary-provider call
  and does not gather tailoring-time remote history. The configs still name
  their normal runner runtime (currently `claude`); creation does not prove
  future runner-provider access.
- **Repository-tailored six** — `entire runner setup --yes` creates the same
  six, gathers repository signal, calls the selected summary provider once, and
  rewrites the prompt templates it can improve. Default gathering reads local
  repository/checkpoint evidence, uses `gh` for PR/issue history when available,
  and uses the authenticated Entire API for trail history when available. Those
  remote tiers are best-effort, but the gathered context and current templates
  are sent to the selected summary provider. If the user wants local repository
  signal only, offer `entire runner setup --yes --sources repo`; it still makes
  the one provider call. When no summary provider is configured, the CLI may
  select one and persist that selection locally; an explicit, verified
  `--agent <name>` chooses one for this run without saving it. Include that
  possible settings write in the approval discussion.

Do not name a tailoring provider unless the user selected one or the installed
CLI verifies it is summary-capable. `--agent` chooses the text-generation agent
for this run; it is not a new runner type.

### Approval and ignore remediation

Show the exact repository path, exact command, expected six files, and the
provider/API implications. Ask for explicit approval and wait. A general request
to audit or bootstrap the repository is not approval to create runner files.

Immediately before an approved setup, re-run the check. It uses
`git check-ignore -v --no-index` against expected runner paths that are not
already tracked; tracked files remain visible regardless of an ignore rule,
while nonexistent pre-setup paths still expose rules that would hide newly
created files. If `runner_ignore_match` is non-empty:

1. Report the exact ignore source, line, pattern, and matched path.
2. Keep `remediate_runner_ignore` separate from runner setup and ask for
   separate approval for the proposed repository-owned fix.
3. For a global `.entire/` rule, prefer a narrow repository `.gitignore`
   exception that re-includes `.entire/`, `.entire/runners/`, and the JSON
   files when that matches repository policy. Do not edit global Git config.
4. Do not use `git add -f`, stage files, or claim ignored files are trackable.
5. Verify `git check-ignore -v --no-index` no longer matches, then present the
   runner setup approval again because the reviewed repository state changed.

### Create and verify after approval

Run exactly the approved supported command from the verified worktree. Do not
run an unflagged interactive setup on the user's behalf:

```bash
entire runner setup --defaults-only
# or
entire runner setup --yes
```

Then re-run `repository-bootstrap check --format json` and verify all of these:

1. `runner_worktree_count` is six and every path in
   `expected_default_runner_files` is a regular JSON file whose `id` matches its
   filename (`runner_default_set_status=complete`).
2. `runner_ignore_match` is empty and `runner_trackable=true`.
3. `runner_git_status` shows the six paths as untracked or modified; an empty
   status does not prove newly created files are visible.
4. `runner_state=uncommitted-visible` and `runner_count=0` until a later,
   separately approved commit records them.

Only then report that the six files were created and are visible for review.
Do not call them committed, do not claim all six were tailored unless the setup
output and file changes prove that, and never report success for ignored files.

### Plan

Emit a deterministic, non-executable plan to stdout:

```bash
bash <skill-dir>/scripts/repository-bootstrap plan --repo . > /tmp/repo.plan
```

The plan contains a repository fingerprint and action identifiers, never shell
commands. It separates:

- `safe`: narrow protective Git configuration fixes supported by this draft;
- `decision`: work that needs repository intent or user confirmation;
- `unsafe`: contradictory identity or topology that blocks apply.

Generating a plan does not mutate the repository. Redirecting stdout to a plan
file is an explicit caller-side write outside the repository. When presenting a
plan to the user, reproduce the complete plan block—including
`ENTIRE_REPOSITORY_BOOTSTRAP_PLAN_V1` and its fingerprint—before interpreting
the actions. The version and fingerprint are part of the review contract, not
internal noise that can be summarized away.

### Apply

Apply only reviewed safe actions:

```bash
bash <skill-dir>/scripts/repository-bootstrap apply \
  --repo . \
  --plan /tmp/repo.plan \
  --yes \
  --allow disable_upstream_push
```

Apply requires all of the following:

1. an exact versioned plan header;
2. a fingerprint matching the repository's current facts;
3. `--yes`;
4. an individual `--allow <action-id>` for every safe action;
5. no unsafe item in the plan;
6. the action's live preconditions still hold.

The only safe actions in this draft are:

- `disable_upstream_push`: set `remote.upstream.pushurl` to `DISABLED` when upstream exists and is not already disabled;
- `set_origin_fetch_refspec`: add the ordinary heads refspec to a bare or bare-worktree repository when origin exists and has no fetch refspec.

Do not broaden apply by constructing commands from plan content or by using
`eval`. Unknown action identifiers are an error.

## Repository identity rules

- `origin` is the user's writable repository and owns Trails, task branches,
  checkpoints, runners, and builds.
- `upstream` is the canonical project. Its push URL must be `DISABLED`.
- Never query upstream as though it were the Trail repository.
- A configured checkpoint repository with a different owner from origin is not
  an automatic fix. Current Entire behavior may ignore it; report the mismatch
  and let the user choose a same-owner configuration or the origin default.
- The required Entire-centered topology is: `origin` is the `entire://` URL,
  `github-origin` is direct GitHub access to the same owner/repository, and
  `upstream` remains canonical and push-disabled.
- A direct GitHub origin is a valid observed state but not the desired final
  state under the default policy. Report `adopt_entire_mirror` as a decision.
- Matching mirror identities and read reachability still do not prove write
  access. Prove that later with an explicitly authorized normal task-branch
  push, then verify the forwarded SHA through `github-origin`.
- Do not automatically route work to `entire/unmirrored/*` when GitHub is
  unavailable. That is a deliberate Entire-native publication choice.

## Decisions this skill never makes

Report these as decisions and stop before acting:

- initialize a repository or create its first commit;
- add, rename, remove, or rewrite a remote;
- enable Entire or install/adopt Graph;
- authenticate, change contexts, or prove write access;
- change checkpoint settings;
- adopt or remove a mirror, including renaming the existing origin;
- stage, stash, clean, reset, or otherwise alter dirty work;
- create a branch, worktree, Trail, checkpoint, build, PR, or comment;
- select a runner setup mode for the user, create runner files without the
  exact approval above, or stage/commit created runner files.

## Handoff to task setup

Repository readiness does not imply task readiness. After facts and decisions
are reviewed, hand the verified repository identity to the later task-bootstrap
workflow. That workflow owns branch/worktree reuse, origin publication, Trail
creation and verification, and its mandatory stop before development begins.

## Exit codes

- `0`: no planned work;
- `2`: safe automatic fixes are available;
- `3`: one or more user decisions remain;
- `4`: unsafe or contradictory topology blocks apply;
- `1`: usage, dependency, stale-plan, or execution error.
---
name: commit
description: Stage changes and commit with a properly formatted conventional commit message. Optionally push. Use when the user says commit / checkpoint this, when completing a task, or after any substantial change. Always use this skill to commit — never run git commit directly.
user-invocable: true
disable-model-invocation: false
---

# Commit

Stage relevant changes and create a commit using the conventional commits format.
Always use this skill instead of running `git commit` directly — this ensures
the message format is consistent across every tool (OpenCode, Claude Code, Codex).

## When to Use

- **Invoke** (`/commit`) after completing every task — this is the final step of every task
- **Invoke** (`/commit --push`) to commit and push in one step
- **AI must use this skill** whenever a commit is needed — never run `git commit -m` directly
- **AI should suggest** when: user says "commit", "save my changes", "checkpoint",
  "commit this", "commit and push", "push my changes", or a task's acceptance criteria say "committed using /commit skill"

## Commit Message Format

```
<type>(<scope>): <description>
```

**Types:**
- `feat` — new feature or capability
- `fix` — bug fix
- `chore` — build, config, dependency, tooling change (no production code change)
- `docs` — documentation only
- `test` — adding or updating tests
- `refactor` — code restructuring with no behaviour change
- `perf` — performance improvement

**Scope** is derived from the project structure. Use the most descriptive scope for the files changed. Scope is optional for small repos or when the change spans the whole repo.

**Examples:**
```
feat(api): add pagination to list endpoint
fix(auth): handle expired refresh tokens
test(search): add round-trip tests for index serialization
chore(ci): update release workflow
refactor(core): extract filter logic into separate function
docs: update CHANGELOG for new feature
```

## Steps

1. Run `git status` to see all changed/untracked files
2. Run `git diff --staged` (or `git diff` if nothing staged) to understand exactly what changed
3. Group related files — do not commit unrelated changes in one commit
4. Stage the relevant files: `git add <specific files>`
5. Draft a commit message following the format above
6. Show the message to the user and confirm before committing
7. Run `git commit -m "<message>"`

### Optional: Push (when `--push` is passed or user asks to push)

8. Push branch to remote:
   - If branch has no upstream: `git push -u origin <branch>`
   - Otherwise: `git push`
9. Run `git status` to verify clean state

## Rules

- **Always use this skill** — never run `git commit` directly without it
- `<type>(<scope>): <description>` — lowercase description, under 72 chars total
- No period at the end
- Description says what changed, not how (the diff shows how)
- **No task IDs, priority labels, or PRD metadata** — no "P0", "TASK-001:", "(PAG-004)"
- Do not stage secrets (`.env`, credentials files)
- Do not use force push
- Stage specific files — never blindly `git add .` without reviewing what's being staged
- **No Co-Authored-By trailers** — do not append `Co-Authored-By` lines to commit messages
- If unsure about the message, show 2-3 options and ask the user to pick
---
name: push-branch
description: Push the current local branch to its remote upstream safely. Use when the user says push / push this branch, or when a branch is ready to publish for PR creation, review, or handoff.
user-invocable: true
disable-model-invocation: false
---

# Push Branch

Publish the current branch without changing history unexpectedly.

## Do

- Confirm the current branch is not the protected base branch.
- Check whether the branch already has an upstream.
- Resolve the exact outgoing commit range before pushing. For an existing
  upstream, compare its verified remote tip with `HEAD`. For a first publish,
  compare the verified branch base with `HEAD`. If the remote tip or branch base
  cannot be established reliably, report that uncertainty before pushing.
- Inspect every commit in that outgoing range for changes to `.entire`,
  `.codex`, `.claude`, `.opencode`, `AGENT.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `GEMINI.md`, or
  `CLAUDE.md`. Inspect commit history rather than only the final tree diff so a
  file that was added and later reverted is still disclosed.
- When outgoing commits touch any of those paths, show the exact paths and ask
  whether they are intentionally part of this push. Path names alone do not
  imply that a change is personal: runner configuration and agent instructions
  are often legitimate repository changes. Wait for a clear answer before
  pushing.
- If the user confirms the paths are intentional, continue with the normal push.
  Treat that answer as confirmation of those files only; it does not authorize a
  different remote, branch, force-push, or history rewrite.
- If the user says they are not intentional, stop before pushing and offer a
  separate remediation. Do not silently unstage files, drop commits, rewrite
  history, create branches, or add ignore rules.
- Keep worktree-only evidence separate. Untracked, staged, or unstaged changes
  that are not committed are not part of a push; leave them untouched and do not
  ask whether they are part of the outgoing push.
- Use a normal push for existing upstreams.
- Use `git push -u origin <branch>` for first publish.
- Do not force-push unless the user explicitly requested it.

## Output

- Branch pushed.
- Remote/upstream used.
- Any Entire or agent-configuration paths the user confirmed as intentional.
- Any push failure and the exact next action needed.

const repos = [
"/Users/muskanpaliwal/dotfiles",
"/Users/muskanpaliwal/notes",
"/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/AI-Tic-Tac-Toe",
"/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/contribution-dashboard",
"/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/entire-lens/main",
"/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/go-git-cli/main"
];
const script = `set -u
printf 'BRANCH\\t'; git branch --show-current
printf 'HEAD\\t'; git rev-parse HEAD
printf 'ORIGIN\\t'; git remote get-url origin
printf 'UPSTREAM_PUSH\\t'; git remote get-url --push upstream 2>/dev/null || true
printf 'WORKTREES\\n'; git worktree list --porcelain
printf 'STAGED\\n'; git diff --cached --name-status
printf 'STATUS\\n'; git status --short --untracked-files=all
printf 'RUNNER_JSON_COUNT\\t'; find .entire/runners -maxdepth 1 -type f -name '*.json' 2>/dev/null | wc -l | tr -d ' '
printf '\\nRUNNER_FILES\\n'; find .entire/runners -maxdepth 1 -type f -name '*.json' 2>/dev/null | LC_ALL=C sort
printf 'RUNNER_IDS\\n'
for f in .entire/runners/*.json; do
  test -f "$f" || continue
  printf '%s\\t' "$f"
  jq -er '.id' "$f"
done
printf 'GIT_VISIBLE\\n'; git status --short --untracked-files=all -- .entire/runners
printf 'CREDENTIAL_SCAN\\n'
rg -n -i '(api[_-]?key|access[_-]?token|secret|password|private[_-]?key|authorization)[[:space:]]*[:=][[:space:]]*["'\"'\"'][^"'\"'\"']{8,}' .entire/runners 2>/dev/null || true`;
const results = await Promise.all(repos.map(repo => tools.exec_command({
  cmd: script,
  workdir: repo,
  yield_time_ms: 10000,
  max_output_tokens: 10000
})));
results.forEach((r,i) => text(`REPO ${repos[i]}\n${r.output}\nEXIT ${r.exit_code}`));

printf 'BRANCH\t'; git branch --show-current
printf 'HEAD\t'; git rev-parse HEAD
printf 'ORIGIN\t'; git remote get-url origin
printf 'UPSTREAM_PUSH\t'; git remote get-url --push upstream 2>/dev/null || true
printf 'WORKTREES\n'; git worktree list --porcelain
printf 'STAGED\n'; git diff --cached --name-status
printf 'STATUS\n'; git status --short --untracked-files=all
printf 'RUNNER_JSON_COUNT\t'; find .entire/runners -maxdepth 1 -type f -name '*.json' 2>/dev/null | wc -l | tr -d ' '
printf '\nRUNNER_FILES\n'; find .entire/runners -maxdepth 1 -type f -name '*.json' 2>/dev/null | LC_ALL=C sort
printf 'RUNNER_IDS\n'
for f in .entire/runners/*.json; do
  test -f "$f" || continue
  printf '%s\t' "$f"
  jq -er '.id' "$f"
done
printf 'GIT_VISIBLE\n'; git status --short --untracked-files=all -- .entire/runners
printf 'CREDENTIAL_SCAN\n'
rg -n -i '(api[_-]?key|access[_-]?token|secret|password|private[_-]?key|authorization)[[:space:]]*[:=][[:space:]]*["'"'"'][^"'"'"']{8,}' .entire/runners 2>/dev/null || true
